title: Ἀγαμέμνονος τραῦμα
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The Muses’ answer comes first: the first to stand against Agamemnon is Iphidamas, a son of Antenor who came to Troy straight from his wedding. His spear bends on the silver of Agamemnon’s belt, and Agamemnon kills him with the sword and begins to strip him. Iphidamas’ elder brother Coön wounds Agamemnon through the arm, but Agamemnon kills him over his brother’s body. Agamemnon goes on fighting until the wound dries, then pain like a woman’s labour seizes him; he tells the chiefs to defend the ships and drives off. Hector rallies the Trojans and Lycians and cuts down the Danaan leaders and then the army, like a storm on the sea. The Achaeans would have been driven into the ships, but Odysseus calls Diomedes to stand with him, and the two of them strike down Thymbraeus and Molion and turn the Trojans back, so that the Achaeans breathe again.

sentences.t:
Ἰφιδάμας Ἀντηνορίδης ἠΰς τε μέγας τε
ὃς τράφη ἐν Θρῄκῃ ἐριβώλακι μητέρι μήλων·
sentences.tr:
Iphidamas Antēnoridēs ēÿs te megas te
hos traphē en Thrēikēi eribōlaki mēteri mēlōn·
sentences.l:
Iphidamas, Antenor’s-son, both good and great,
who was reared in Thrace, rich-soiled, mother of sheep;
sentences.i: Iphidamas, son of Antenor, both good and great, who was reared in Thrace of the rich soil, the mother of flocks;
sentences.n: This is the Muses’ answer to the question that closed the last part: the first to stand against Agamemnon was Iphidamas, a son of Antenor. Ἀντηνορίδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Antenor’, like Ἀτρεΐδης. ἠΰς is the epic form of ἐΰς ‘good’, and ἠΰς τε μέγας τε ‘both good and great’ is a stock phrase of praise. τράφη is the unaugmented aorist passive of τρέφω ‘rear’ (Attic ἐτράφη), so ‘was reared’; ὃς here is the relative ‘who’. ἐριβώλακι ‘rich-soiled’ is a stock epithet of lands and agrees with Θρῄκῃ ‘in Thrace’; μητέρι μήλων ‘mother of sheep’ stands beside it as a second description of the land, μῆλα being small livestock, sheep and goats. The unit stops at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
Κισσῆς τόν γ’ ἔθρεψε δόμοις ἔνι τυτθὸν ἐόντα
μητροπάτωρ, ὃς τίκτε Θεανὼ καλλιπάρῃον·
sentences.tr:
Kissēs ton g’ ethrepse domois eni tytthon eonta
mētropatōr, hos tikte Theanō kalliparēion·
sentences.l:
Cisses him indeed reared in the house, a little child being,
his mother’s father, who begot Theano, fair-cheeked;
sentences.i: Cisses, his mother’s father, who was the father of fair-cheeked Theano, reared him in his house when he was a small child;
sentences.n: A family note to say who brought Iphidamas up: Cisses, the father of his mother, not Antenor. Κισσῆς is the nominative with the Ionic ending -ης; τόν γ’ is ‘him’ with γε giving the pronoun a little stress. δόμοις ἔνι is ‘in the house’: ἔνι (= ἐνί) stands after its noun, so its accent moves back, and τυτθὸν ἐόντα ‘being little’ agrees with τόν. μητροπάτωρ is ‘mother’s father’, built from μήτηρ and πατήρ. ὃς τίκτε is ‘who begot’, τίκτω said of the father; Θεανώ is a woman’s name, and the text says no more of her here. καλλιπάρῃον ‘fair-cheeked’ is the stock epithet in its Homeric spelling (παρειά ‘cheek’).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἥβης ἐρικυδέος ἵκετο μέτρον,
αὐτοῦ μιν κατέρυκε, δίδου δ’ ὅ γε θυγατέρα ἥν·
sentences.tr:
autar epei rh’ hēbēs erikydeos hiketo metron,
autou min kateryke, didou d’ ho ge thygatera hēn·
sentences.l:
But when then of glorious youth he reached the measure,
there he held him back, and was giving, he for his part, his own daughter;
sentences.i: But when he reached the measure of glorious youth, he kept him there, and gave him his own daughter;
sentences.n: The subject of both lines is still Cisses: when the boy came of age, his grandfather kept him at home and gave him a daughter in marriage. ῥ’ is ῥα, the particle ἄρα ‘then’, and ἥβης μέτρον ‘the measure of youth’ is the age at which a boy becomes a man, with ἐρικυδέος ‘glorious’ agreeing with ἥβης. ἵκετο is an unaugmented aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘reach’. αὐτοῦ is the adverb ‘on the spot, there’, not the pronoun. δίδου is the imperfect ‘was giving’, and ὅ γε ‘he for his part’ points back at Cisses. ἥν is the possessive ‘his own’, easily taken for a relative. Line 226 is the line used of Bellerophon at 6.192, with a raised dot where the other had a comma. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: the first syllable of θυγατέρα, short in ordinary speech, is lengthened to fill the longum of the fifth foot.

sentences.t:
γήμας δ’ ἐκ θαλάμοιο μετὰ κλέος ἵκετ’ Ἀχαιῶν
σὺν δυοκαίδεκα νηυσὶ κορωνίσιν, αἵ οἱ ἕποντο.
sentences.tr:
gēmas d’ ek thalamoio meta kleos hiket’ Achaiōn
syn dyokaideka nēusi korōnisin, hai hoi heponto.
sentences.l:
and having married, from the bridal chamber, after the fame of the Achaeans he came,
with twelve curved ships, which followed him.
sentences.i: Once he had married, he came from the bridal chamber after the fame of the Achaeans, with twelve curved ships that followed him.
sentences.n: Iphidamas left his wedding to join the war, bringing a fleet of his own. γήμας is the aorist participle of γαμέω ‘marry’ (said of the man), and ἐκ θαλάμοιο ‘out of the bridal chamber’ (the epic genitive -οιο) shows how soon he left. μετὰ κλέος … Ἀχαιῶν ‘after the fame of the Achaeans’ means he came in pursuit of the glory the expedition was winning; κλέος is ‘report, fame’, both at once. δυοκαίδεκα is ‘twelve’ in the old spelling (δύο καί δέκα; Attic δώδεκα). νηυσὶ κορωνίσιν ‘curved ships’ is a stock phrase, and ἕποντο is the unaugmented imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’.

sentences.t:
τὰς μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἐν Περκώτῃ λίπε νῆας ἐΐσας,
αὐτὰρ ὃ πεζὸς ἐὼν ἐς Ἴλιον εἰληλούθει·
sentences.tr:
tas men epeit’ en Perkōtēi lipe nēas eïsas,
autar ho pezos eōn es Ilion eilēlouthei·
sentences.l:
Those then, in Percote, he left, the ships, well-balanced,
but he, on foot being, to Ilios had come;
sentences.i: He left those ships behind in Percote, the well-balanced ships, but he himself had come to Ilios on foot;
sentences.n: He did not bring the fleet to Troy itself: the ships stayed at Percote, a town in the Troad, and he walked the rest of the way. τὰς … νῆας is ‘those ships’, and ἐΐσας is a stock epithet of ships whose sense is not certain; ‘well-balanced’ is the usual guess. αὐτὰρ ὃ is ‘but he’, with ὃ a pronoun, and πεζὸς ἐών ‘being on foot’ is set against the ships. εἰληλούθει is the pluperfect of ἔρχομαι, ‘had come’ (Attic ἐληλύθει). The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: the last syllable of Ἴλιον counts long before εἰληλούθει, as if that word still began with a consonant (the old digamma), and the fifth foot is a spondee.

sentences.t: ὅς ῥα τότ’ Ἀτρεΐδεω Ἀγαμέμνονος ἀντίον ἦλθεν.
sentences.tr: hos rha tot’ Atreïdeō Agamemnonos antion ēlthen.
sentences.l: who then, at that time, against Atreus’-son Agamemnon came.
sentences.i: This was the man who at that time came against Agamemnon, the son of Atreus.
sentences.n: The relative ὅς at the head of a sentence, ὅς ῥα, picks up the man just described and starts a new statement: ‘and he it was who…’. ῥα is the particle ἄρα, and τότ’ is ‘at that time’. ἀντίον ἦλθεν ‘came against’ takes the genitive, here the epic form Ἀτρεΐδεω (= Ἀτρεΐδου). Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’ is the usual name for Agamemnon.

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ὅτε δὴ σχεδὸν ἦσαν ἐπ’ ἀλλήλοισιν ἰόντες,
Ἀτρεΐδης μὲν ἅμαρτε, παραὶ δέ οἱ ἐτράπετ’ ἔγχος,
Ἰφιδάμας δὲ κατὰ ζώνην θώρηκος ἔνερθε
νύξ’, ἐπὶ δ’ αὐτὸς ἔρεισε βαρείῃ χειρὶ πιθήσας·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ hote dē schedon ēsan ep’ allēloisin iontes,
Atreïdēs men hamarte, parai de hoi etrapet’ enchos,
Iphidamas de kata zōnēn thōrēkos enerthe
nyx’, epi d’ autos ereise bareiēi cheiri pithēsas·
sentences.l:
And when they were near, going against one another,
Atreus’-son missed, and aside for him turned the spear,
and Iphidamas, on the girdle, below the breastplate,
stabbed, and upon it himself pressed, trusting in his heavy hand;
sentences.i: And when they were near, advancing on one another, the son of Atreus missed, and the spear turned aside from him, and Iphidamas stabbed at the belt below the breastplate, and pressed in on it himself, trusting in his heavy hand;
sentences.n: The two heroes cast first: Agamemnon’s spear goes wide, and Iphidamas’ strikes at the belt below the breastplate. The first line is the line that opens the first meeting of the armies at 3.15 and the clash at 5.850. ἅμαρτε is the unaugmented aorist of ἁμαρτάνω ‘miss’. παραί is a by-form of παρά ‘aside’, ἐτράπετ’ is the aorist middle of τρέπω ‘turn’, so ‘turned (itself) aside’, and οἱ ‘for him’ is a dative. νύξ’ is νύξε, aorist of νύσσω ‘stab’. ἐπὶ … ἔρεισε is a tmesis (ἐπέρεισε ‘pressed on’), and πιθήσας is the aorist participle of πείθομαι ‘trust, rely on’, with the dative βαρείῃ χειρί ‘heavy hand’. ζώνη is ‘girdle’ in the word-for-word line, and it is the piece the next unit calls a ζωστήρ ‘belt’; the free English says ‘belt’ for both. The unit stops at the raised dot, at the end of line 235.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἔτορε ζωστῆρα παναίολον, ἀλλὰ πολὺ πρὶν
ἀργύρῳ ἀντομένη μόλιβος ὣς ἐτράπετ’ αἰχμή.
sentences.tr:
oud’ etore zōstēra panaiolon, alla poly prin
argyrōi antomenē molibos hōs etrapet’ aichmē.
sentences.l:
and he did not pierce the all-glancing belt, but well before
against silver meeting, like lead it was turned, the point.
sentences.i: He did not pierce the belt, all-glancing as it was, but long before that the point met silver and was turned aside like lead.
sentences.n: Iphidamas’ blow fails: the point meets silver and bends back, so the thrust never reaches the flesh. ἔτορε is an aorist of a verb meaning ‘pierce, bore through’ (stem τορ-). παναίολον ‘all-glancing’ is the belt’s epithet; it is not certain whether it means gleaming or many-coloured. ἀλλὰ πολὺ πρίν is ‘but long before’, and ἀργύρῳ is plain ‘silver’; the text does not say what the silver is part of, and it is read as silver on the belt. ἀντομένη ‘meeting’ goes with αἰχμή ‘point’ and is feminine; μόλιβος is ‘lead’, and ὣς stands after its noun, ‘like lead’. ἐτράπετ’ is the verb of line 233, now said of the point as it bends.

sentences.t:
καὶ τό γε χειρὶ λαβὼν εὐρὺ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
ἕλκ’ ἐπὶ οἷ μεμαὼς ὥς τε λίς, ἐκ δ’ ἄρα χειρὸς
σπάσσατο·
sentences.tr:
kai to ge cheiri labōn eury kreiōn Agamemnōn
helk’ epi hoi memaōs hōs te lis, ek d’ ara cheiros
spassato·
sentences.i: Wide-ruling Agamemnon took hold of it in his hand and dragged it toward himself, eager as a lion, and wrenched it out of the hand;
sentences.n: Agamemnon seizes the spear that failed to pierce him and pulls it out of Iphidamas’ grip. τό γε is ‘that’ (the spear, understood from ἔγχος and αἰχμή above), and εὐρὺ κρείων is printed as two words and is the stock epithet ‘wide-ruling’. ἕλκ’ is ἕλκε, imperfect ‘was dragging’, with ἐπὶ οἷ ‘toward himself’ (οἷ is the reflexive dative of ἕ); μεμαώς is ‘eager’, and λίς is ‘lion’. ἐκ … σπάσσατο is a tmesis (ἐκσπάσσατο ‘wrenched out’), aorist middle of σπάω. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of line 240.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄορι πλῆξ’ αὐχένα, λῦσε δὲ γυῖα.
sentences.tr: ton d’ aori plēx’ auchena, lyse de guia.
sentences.l: and him with the sword he struck on the neck, and loosed his limbs.
sentences.i: and struck him on the neck with his sword, and loosed his limbs.
sentences.n: Agamemnon kills Iphidamas with a sword-stroke to the neck. λῦσε δὲ γυῖα ‘and loosed his limbs’ is the usual way of saying that a man was killed: the strength goes out of him. πλῆξ’ is πλῆξε, aorist of πλήσσω ‘strike’, ἄορι is the dative of instrument, ‘with the sword’, and αὐχένα ‘neck’ names the part struck.

sentences.t:
ὣς ὃ μὲν αὖθι πεσὼν κοιμήσατο χάλκεον ὕπνον
οἰκτρὸς ἀπὸ μνηστῆς ἀλόχου, ἀστοῖσιν ἀρήγων,
κουριδίης, ἧς οὔ τι χάριν ἴδε, πολλὰ δ’ ἔδωκε·
sentences.tr:
hōs ho men authi pesōn koimēsato chalkeon hypnon
oiktros apo mnēstēs alochou, astoisin arēgōn,
kouridiēs, hēs ou ti charin ide, polla d’ edōke·
sentences.i: So he fell on the spot and slept a bronze sleep, pitiable, far from his wedded wife, though he had come to help the townsmen — his wedded wife, of whom he had no joy, though he had given much for her;
sentences.n: The poet stops to pity the dead man, a husband of a few days who died far from home. χάλκεον ὕπνον ‘a bronze sleep’ is death by the bronze weapon, ὕπνος ‘sleep’ with its own verb κοιμήσατο (aorist middle of κοιμάω ‘put to sleep’). αὖθι is ‘on the spot’. ἀρήγων ‘helping’ and ἀστοῖσιν ‘townsmen’: the citizens of Troy, for whom he had come to fight (the Greek says only ‘townsmen’, with no ‘his’). μνηστῆς and κουριδίης both mean ‘wedded’ (the first ‘wooed’, the second ‘lawfully married’), and the Greek says it twice, so the English does too. χάριν ἴδε is ‘saw favour’: χάρις is ‘favour, delight, thanks’, and the sense is that he had no joy or return from her. πολλὰ δ’ ἔδωκε ‘though much he gave’ looks forward to the bride-gifts in the next two lines.

sentences.t:
πρῶθ’ ἑκατὸν βοῦς δῶκεν, ἔπειτα δὲ χίλι’ ὑπέστη
αἶγας ὁμοῦ καὶ ὄϊς, τά οἱ ἄσπετα ποιμαίνοντο.
sentences.tr:
prōth’ hekaton bous dōken, epeita de chili’ hypestē
aigas homou kai oïs, ta hoi aspeta poimainonto.
sentences.l:
First a hundred cattle he gave, and then a thousand he undertook,
goats together and sheep, which for him boundless were being tended.
sentences.i: First he gave a hundred cattle, and then he undertook to give a thousand goats and sheep together, which were being tended for him in boundless numbers.
sentences.n: This is the much he gave: a hundred cattle first, and a promise of a thousand goats and sheep more. πρῶθ’ is πρῶτα ‘first’, βοῦς is the accusative plural ‘cattle’, and χίλι’ is χίλια ‘a thousand’. ὑπέστη is the aorist of ὑφίσταμαι ‘undertake’: he bound himself to pay. αἶγας ὁμοῦ καὶ ὄϊς is ‘goats together and sheep’, ὄϊς being the accusative plural of ὄϊς ‘sheep’. τά is the relative ‘which’, ἄσπετα ‘boundless’ literally ‘not to be told’, and ποιμαίνοντο is the passive of ποιμαίνω ‘tend as a shepherd’.

sentences.t:
δὴ τότε γ’ Ἀτρεΐδης Ἀγαμέμνων ἐξενάριξε,
βῆ δὲ φέρων ἀν’ ὅμιλον Ἀχαιῶν τεύχεα καλά.
sentences.tr:
dē tote g’ Atreïdēs Agamemnōn exenarixe,
bē de pherōn an’ homilon Achaiōn teuchea kala.
sentences.l:
Then indeed Atreus’-son Agamemnon despoiled him,
and went, bearing through the throng of the Achaeans, the fine armour.
sentences.i: Then the son of Atreus, Agamemnon, stripped him of his armour, and went off through the throng of the Achaeans carrying the fine armour.
sentences.n: The aside over, the action resumes: Agamemnon strips the body and carries the armour off. The object of ἐξενάριξε is Iphidamas, left unsaid because the killing has already been told, so the verb means only the stripping: ‘despoiled’. δὴ τότε γ’ is ‘then, indeed’, with γε adding stress. βῆ is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω ‘go’, ἀν’ is ἀνά ‘up and down, through’, and ὅμιλον is ‘throng’. τεύχεα καλά ‘fine armour’ is the object of φέρων ‘bearing’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησε Κόων ἀριδείκετος ἀνδρῶν
πρεσβυγενὴς Ἀντηνορίδης, κρατερόν ῥά ἑ πένθος
ὀφθαλμοὺς ἐκάλυψε κασιγνήτοιο πεσόντος.
sentences.tr:
ton d’ hōs oun enoēse Koōn arideiketos andrōn
presbygenēs Antēnoridēs, krateron rha he penthos
ophthalmous ekalypse kasignētoio pesontos.
sentences.l:
Him then as he noticed, Coön, most conspicuous of men,
eldest-born son of Antenor, strong grief then him
his eyes covered, at his brother having fallen.
sentences.i: And when Coön, most distinguished of men, the eldest son of Antenor, saw him, strong grief covered his eyes at the fall of his brother.
sentences.n: A new fighter enters: Coön, Iphidamas’ elder brother, who sees the body being stripped. τὸν δ’ ὡς οὖν ἐνόησε ‘and when he noticed him’ opens a sentence whose subject follows: Κόων, with the stock epithet ἀριδείκετος ‘most conspicuous’ in the word-for-word line and ‘most distinguished’ in the English. πρεσβυγενής is ‘eldest-born’, so Coön is the elder son of Ἀντηνορίδης ‘the son of Antenor’. ῥά is ἄρα, and ἑ is the accusative ‘him’, set beside ὀφθαλμούς ‘eyes’ in the way Greek names the person and then the part: ‘grief covered him, the eyes’. The grief is a darkness over the eyes. κασιγνήτοιο πεσόντος is ‘his brother having fallen’, the epic genitive -οιο.

sentences.t:
στῆ δ’ εὐρὰξ σὺν δουρὶ λαθὼν Ἀγαμέμνονα δῖον,
νύξε δέ μιν κατὰ χεῖρα μέσην ἀγκῶνος ἔνερθε,
ἀντικρὺ δὲ διέσχε φαεινοῦ δουρὸς ἀκωκή.
sentences.tr:
stē d’ eurax syn douri lathōn Agamemnona dion,
nyxe de min kata cheira mesēn ankōnos enerthe,
antikry de diesche phaeinou douros akōkē.
sentences.l:
and he stood sideways, with spear, having escaped the notice of heavenly Agamemnon,
and stabbed him in the arm, in the middle, below the elbow,
and right through passed the tip of the shining spear.
sentences.i: He took his stand to one side with his spear, unseen by heavenly Agamemnon, and stabbed him in the middle of the arm below the elbow, and the tip of the shining spear passed right through.
sentences.n: Coön strikes from the side, while Agamemnon’s attention is elsewhere, and the spear goes through his forearm below the elbow. στῆ is the unaugmented aorist of ἵστημι ‘stand’, here ‘took his stand’. εὐρὰξ is a rare word, usually taken as ‘sideways, aslant’. λαθών is the aorist participle of λανθάνω ‘escape the notice of’, with the accusative Ἀγαμέμνονα δῖον (δῖος ‘heavenly’). νύξε is the aorist of νύσσω ‘stab’; χεῖρα here is the arm below the elbow joint, and κατά with the accusative gives the place of the blow. διέσχε is ‘passed through’, and ἀντικρύ ‘right through’; ἀκωκή is ‘tip’.

sentences.t: ῥίγησέν τ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr: rhigēsen t’ ar’ epeita anax andrōn Agamemnōn·
sentences.l: And shuddered then, lord of men, Agamemnon;
sentences.i: and then Agamemnon, lord of men, shuddered;
sentences.n: Agamemnon’s body reacts to the wound before he does. ῥίγησε is the aorist of ῥιγέω ‘shudder’, from ῥῖγος ‘chill’, and the Greek gives no cause beyond the pain. τ’ ἄρ’ is the particles τε ἄρα, ‘and then’, and ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is the stock epithet of Agamemnon.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὧς ἀπέληγε μάχης ἠδὲ πτολέμοιο,
ἀλλ’ ἐπόρουσε Κόωνι ἔχων ἀνεμοτρεφὲς ἔγχος.
sentences.tr:
all’ oud’ hōs apelēge machēs ēde ptolemoio,
all’ eporouse Koōni echōn anemotrephes enchos.
sentences.l:
but not even so did he cease from fighting and from war,
but rushed at Coön, holding a wind-nurtured spear.
sentences.i: but even so he did not stop fighting or making war, and rushed at Coön, holding his wind-nurtured spear.
sentences.n: The wounded king keeps fighting and goes straight for Coön. ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὧς is ‘but not even so’, ἀπέληγε is the imperfect of ἀπολήγω ‘cease from’ (with the genitive μάχης ἠδὲ πτολέμοιο, ‘fighting and war’), and ἐπόρουσε is the aorist of ἐπορούω ‘rush upon’, with the dative Κόωνι. ἀνεμοτρεφές is built from ἄνεμος ‘wind’ and τρέφω ‘nourish’; what it means for a spear is not known, and ‘wind-nurtured’ keeps its parts. ἔχων is ‘holding’.

sentences.t:
ἤτοι ὃ Ἰφιδάμαντα κασίγνητον καὶ ὄπατρον
ἕλκε ποδὸς μεμαώς, καὶ ἀΰτει πάντας ἀρίστους·
sentences.tr:
ētoi ho Iphidamanta kasignēton kai opatron
helke podos memaōs, kai aÿtei pantas aristous·
sentences.l:
Now he, Iphidamas, his brother and born of the same father,
dragged by the foot, eager, and called to all the best;
sentences.i: Now Coön was dragging his brother Iphidamas, born of the same father, by the foot, eager as he was, and he called out to all the best men;
sentences.n: The subject changes here: ὃ is a pronoun, and it is Coön, not Agamemnon: he is dragging his dead brother away by the foot and calling for the best fighters to help him. ἤτοι ‘now, indeed’ is printed as one word. κασίγνητον καὶ ὄπατρον is ‘brother and born of the same father’: ὄπατρος is ὁ- (together) and πατήρ ‘father’. ἕλκε is the imperfect ‘was dragging’, with the genitive ποδός ‘by the foot’; μεμαώς is ‘eager’, and ἀΰτει is the imperfect of ἀϋτέω ‘call out’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἕλκοντ’ ἀν’ ὅμιλον ὑπ’ ἀσπίδος ὀμφαλοέσσης
οὔτησε ξυστῷ χαλκήρεϊ, λῦσε δὲ γυῖα·
sentences.tr:
ton d’ helkont’ an’ homilon hyp’ aspidos omphaloessēs
outēse xystōi chalkēreï, lyse de guia·
sentences.l:
And him, as he dragged through the throng, from beneath the bossed shield
wounded with a polished, bronze-fitted spear, and loosed his limbs;
sentences.i: And as Coön dragged him through the throng, Agamemnon stabbed him from beneath his bossed shield with his polished, bronze-fitted spear, and loosed his limbs;
sentences.n: Agamemnon takes his revenge while Coön is busy with the body: the subject is Agamemnon, understood from the line before, and the object is Coön, ‘him dragging’. ἕλκοντ’ is the participle ἕλκοντα, accusative ‘dragging’. ὑπ’ ἀσπίδος ὀμφαλοέσσης is ‘from beneath the bossed shield’ (ὀμφαλός is the boss at the centre). οὔτησε is the aorist of οὐτάω ‘wound’, and ξυστῷ χαλκήρεϊ ‘polished, bronze-fitted spear’ is the dative of instrument. The second line is word for word the line of 4.469, and λῦσε δὲ γυῖα is again the phrase for killing.

sentences.t: τοῖο δ’ ἐπ’ Ἰφιδάμαντι κάρη ἀπέκοψε παραστάς.
sentences.tr: toio d’ ep’ Iphidamanti karē apekopse parastas.
sentences.l: and over Iphidamas the head of him he cut off, standing beside.
sentences.i: and standing beside him, he cut off his head over Iphidamas.
sentences.n: Coön’s head is cut off as he lies across his brother’s body. τοῖο is the epic genitive of the pronoun, ‘of him’, and it stands before κάρη ‘head’ (a neuter noun), ‘his head’. ἐπ’ Ἰφιδάμαντι is ‘upon, over Iphidamas’, with the dative. ἀπέκοψε is the aorist of ἀποκόπτω ‘cut off’, and παραστάς is the aorist participle of παρίστημι ‘stand beside’. The subject is still Agamemnon.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ Ἀντήνορος υἷες ὑπ’ Ἀτρεΐδῃ βασιλῆϊ
πότμον ἀναπλήσαντες ἔδυν δόμον Ἄϊδος εἴσω.
sentences.tr:
enth’ Antēnoros huies hyp’ Atreïdēi basilēï
potmon anaplēsantes edyn domon Aïdos eisō.
sentences.l:
There Antenor’s sons, beneath Atreus’-son the king,
having filled up their doom, went down into the house of Hades within.
sentences.i: So there the sons of Antenor, at the hands of the king, the son of Atreus, filled up their doom and went down into the house of Hades.
sentences.n: The poet sums up: both of Antenor’s sons are dead. ἔνθ’ is ‘there’, υἷες is the epic nominative plural of υἱός ‘sons’, and ὑπ’ Ἀτρεΐδῃ βασιλῆϊ is ‘beneath the king, Atreus’-son’, ὑπό with the dative saying who overcame them (βασιλῆϊ is the epic dative). πότμον ἀναπλήσαντες is ‘having filled up their doom’: they used up their allotted measure. ἔδυν is the aorist plural of δύω ‘go down into’ (Attic ἔδυσαν), and δόμον Ἄϊδος εἴσω is ‘into the house of Hades’, with εἴσω ‘within’ standing last and δόμον the accusative of the place gone to.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ τῶν ἄλλων ἐπεπωλεῖτο στίχας ἀνδρῶν
ἔγχεΐ τ’ ἄορί τε μεγάλοισί τε χερμαδίοισιν,
ὄφρά οἱ αἷμ’ ἔτι θερμὸν ἀνήνοθεν ἐξ ὠτειλῆς.
sentences.tr:
autar ho tōn allōn epepōleito stichas andrōn
encheï t’ aori te megaloisi te chermadioisin,
ophra hoi haim’ eti thermon anēnothen ex ōteilēs.
sentences.l:
But he, of the other men, was going about the ranks,
with spear and with sword and with great stones,
so long as for him blood still warm welled up from the wound.
sentences.i: But he ranged along the ranks of the other men with spear and sword and great stones, as long as the blood still welled warm from his wound.
sentences.n: Agamemnon, still the subject (αὐτὰρ ὃ ‘but he’), goes on fighting for as long as the wound is fresh. ἐπεπωλεῖτο is the imperfect of ἐπιπωλέομαι ‘go to and fro over’, with στίχας ‘ranks’, and τῶν ἄλλων … ἀνδρῶν is ‘of the other men’. The three weapons are in the dative: ἔγχεϊ ‘spear’, ἄορι ‘sword’, χερμαδίοισιν ‘stones’ (χερμάδια are stones that fill the hand). ὄφρα means ‘as long as’. ἀνήνοθεν is an old perfect used as a present, ‘welled up’, with the dative οἱ ‘for him’ and ἐξ ὠτειλῆς ‘from the wound’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ τὸ μὲν ἕλκος ἐτέρσετο, παύσατο δ’ αἷμα,
ὀξεῖαι δ’ ὀδύναι δῦνον μένος Ἀτρεΐδαο.
sentences.tr:
autar epei to men helkos eterseto, pausato d’ haima,
oxeiai d’ odynai dynon menos Atreïdao.
sentences.l:
But when the wound dried, and the blood ceased,
sharp pains entered the might of Atreus’-son.
sentences.i: But when the wound dried and the blood stopped, sharp pains entered the might of the son of Atreus.
sentences.n: The change comes when the wound dries: the pain, held off while it bled, now sets in. ἐτέρσετο is the imperfect of τέρσομαι ‘be dried up’, and τὸ μὲν ἕλκος ‘the wound, for its part’ is set against the blood, αἷμα. δῦνον is the imperfect of δύνω ‘sink into, enter’, so the pains kept entering, one after another, and μένος ‘might’ is their object. Ἀτρεΐδαο is the epic genitive of Ἀτρεΐδης. The line comes round again, with ὣς for δ’, as the last line of the simile in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ὠδίνουσαν ἔχῃ βέλος ὀξὺ γυναῖκα
δριμύ, τό τε προϊεῖσι μογοστόκοι Εἰλείθυιαι
Ἥρης θυγατέρες πικρὰς ὠδῖνας ἔχουσαι,
ὣς ὀξεῖ’ ὀδύναι δῦνον μένος Ἀτρεΐδαο.
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ an ōdinousan echēi belos oxy gynaika
drimy, to te proïeisi mogostokoi Eileithuiai
Hērēs thygateres pikras ōdinas echousai,
hōs oxei’ odynai dynon menos Atreïdao.
sentences.l:
And as when a sharp shaft takes hold of a woman in labour,
a keen one, which the travail-bringing Eileithyiae send forth,
daughters of Hera, holding bitter pangs,
so sharp pains entered the might of Atreus’-son.
sentences.i: As when a sharp, keen shaft takes hold of a woman in labour — the shaft that the Eileithyiae send, the goddesses of the travail of birth, daughters of Hera, who hold the bitter pangs — so sharp pains entered the might of the son of Atreus.
sentences.n: A simile for the pain: it is like a woman’s labour pains, which are shot into her by the Eileithyiae, the goddesses of childbirth. ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν … ἔχῃ is ‘as when … takes hold’, with ἄν and the subjunctive for what happens whenever it happens, and ὠδίνουσαν is ‘in labour’. βέλος is ‘shaft’, and the pains are pictured as shafts sent by the goddesses; μογοστόκοι is built from μόγος ‘toil, travail’ and τόκος ‘birth’. Ἥρης is the Ionic genitive of Ἥρη, ‘daughters of Hera’. προϊεῖσι is the present of προΐημι ‘send forth’ (Attic προϊᾶσι), and the relative τό ‘which’ has τε after it, which marks the general truth. The last line returns to Agamemnon in nearly the words of line 268 (ὣς for δ’). The line (271) is metrically irregular as transmitted: the first syllable of θυγατέρες, short in ordinary speech, is lengthened to fill the longum of the second foot.

sentences.t:
ἐς δίφρον δ’ ἀνόρουσε, καὶ ἡνιόχῳ ἐπέτελλε
νηυσὶν ἔπι γλαφυρῇσιν ἐλαυνέμεν·
sentences.tr:
es diphron d’ anorouse, kai hēniochōi epetelle
nēusin epi glaphyrēisin elaunemen·
sentences.l:
and into the chariot he leapt up, and to the charioteer gave instructions
to drive on to the hollow ships;
sentences.i: and he leapt up into the chariot and gave the charioteer instructions to drive to the hollow ships;
sentences.n: Agamemnon leaves the fight. ἀνόρουσε is the aorist of ἀνορούω ‘leap up’, and δίφρον is ‘chariot’ here. ἡνιόχῳ is the dative of ἡνίοχος ‘charioteer’, ἐπέτελλε is the imperfect of ἐπιτέλλω ‘give instructions’, and ἐλαυνέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’ (Attic ἐλαύνειν). ἔπι stands after its noun, so its accent moves back; νηυσὶν … γλαφυρῇσιν is ‘the hollow ships’, with the epic dative ending -ῃσιν. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of line 274.

sentences.t: ἤχθετο γὰρ κῆρ.
sentences.tr: ēchtheto gar kēr.
sentences.l: for he was distressed in heart.
sentences.i: for he was distressed at heart.
sentences.n: The reason he leaves: the pain of the wound, as the simile has just shown. ἤχθετο is the imperfect of ἄχθομαι ‘be distressed, weighed down’, and κῆρ is ‘heart’ in the accusative of respect, ‘distressed in his heart’. γάρ gives the reason for the order just given.

sentences.t: ἤϋσεν δὲ διαπρύσιον Δαναοῖσι γεγωνώς·
sentences.tr: ēÿsen de diaprysion Danaoisi gegōnōs·
sentences.l: And he shouted, piercingly, calling to the Danaans:
sentences.i: and he shouted piercingly, calling out to the Danaans:
sentences.n: Before he goes, Agamemnon calls out to the army; the line is word for word the line of 8.227, where Agamemnon shouts to the Danaans in the same way. ἤϋσεν is the aorist of ἀϋτέω ‘shout’, with the diaeresis printed. διαπρύσιον is the adverb ‘piercingly’, γεγωνώς is the perfect participle of γεγωνέω ‘call out so as to be heard’, and Δαναοῖσι is the epic dative ‘to the Danaans’. A speech follows.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι Ἀργείων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες
ὑμεῖς μὲν νῦν νηυσὶν ἀμύνετε ποντοπόροισι
φύλοπιν ἀργαλέην, ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἐμὲ μητίετα Ζεὺς
εἴασε Τρώεσσι πανημέριον πολεμίζειν.
sentences.tr:
ō philoi Argeiōn hēgētores ēde medontes
hymeis men nyn nēusin amynete pontoporoisi
phylopin argaleēn, epei ouk eme mētieta Zeus
eiase Trōessi panēmerion polemizein.
sentences.l:
“O friends, leaders and lords of the Argives,
you indeed now, for the sea-crossing ships, ward off
the grievous battle-din, since not me counsellor Zeus
allowed against the Trojans all day long to fight.”
sentences.i: “Friends, leaders and lords of the Argives: you, for your part, now keep the grievous din of battle away from the sea-crossing ships, since Zeus the counsellor has not allowed me to fight the Trojans all day long.”
sentences.n: Agamemnon hands the defence to his captains: he cannot go on. The first line is the stock address that opens speeches at 2.79, 9.17 and 10.533; ὦ φίλοι is ‘O friends’, and Ἀργείων ἡγήτορες ἠδὲ μέδοντες is ‘leaders and lords of the Argives’. ὑμεῖς μὲν νῦν is ‘you now, for your part’, with no δέ to answer it: the contrast with himself is in the second half. ἀμύνετε is the imperative of ἀμύνω ‘ward off’, with the dative νηυσὶ ποντοπόροισι ‘for the sea-crossing ships’, and φύλοπιν ἀργαλέην is the ‘grievous din of battle’. In the last two lines, the accusative ἐμέ is the subject of πολεμίζειν: εἴασε … πολεμίζειν is ‘allowed (me) to fight’, with the dative Τρώεσσι ‘against the Trojans’ and πανημέριον ‘all day long’. μητίετα Ζεύς is ‘counsellor Zeus’, the epithet translated every time. The Greek carries no quotation marks.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, ἡνίοχος δ’ ἵμασεν καλλίτριχας ἵππους
νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephath’, hēniochos d’ himasen kallitrichas hippous
nēas epi glaphyras·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and the charioteer lashed the fair-maned horses
to the hollow ships;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the charioteer lashed the fair-maned horses to the hollow ships;
sentences.n: The speech ends with the usual closing line. ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘so he spoke’: ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο with the τ made rough before the rough breathing of ἡνίοχος. ἵμασεν is the aorist of ἱμάσσω ‘lash’, from ἱμάς ‘strap, thong’, and καλλίτριχας ἵππους is ‘fair-maned horses’, a stock phrase. νῆας ἔπι γλαφυράς is ‘to the hollow ships’, with ἔπι after its noun and the accusative of goal. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of line 281.

sentences.t: τὼ δ’ οὐκ ἀέκοντε πετέσθην·
sentences.tr: tō d’ ouk aekonte petesthēn·
sentences.l: and the two, not unwilling, flew;
sentences.i: and the pair flew not unwilling;
sentences.n: The litotes ‘not unwilling’ means they went eagerly. τὼ is the dual of the pronoun, ‘the two’ (the pair of horses), with the dual participle ἀέκοντε ‘unwilling’ and the dual verb πετέσθην, aorist of πέτομαι ‘fly’. The Odyssey has this half-line too, at 3.484. The dual here is for the pair of horses, and the next unit goes back to the plural.

sentences.t:
ἄφρεον δὲ στήθεα, ῥαίνοντο δὲ νέρθε κονίῃ
τειρόμενον βασιλῆα μάχης ἀπάνευθε φέροντες.
sentences.tr:
aphreon de stēthea, rhainonto de nerthe koniēi
teiromenon basilēa machēs apaneuthe pherontes.
sentences.l:
and they foamed at the chests, and were sprinkled below with dust,
bearing the worn-down king apart from the battle.
sentences.i: Their chests foamed, and below they were spattered with dust, as they carried the worn-down king away from the battle.
sentences.n: A picture of the speed: foam on the horses’ chests, dust thrown up under them, the wounded king in the car. ἄφρεον is the imperfect of ἀφρέω ‘foam’, with στήθεα ‘chests’ as the accusative of the part. ῥαίνοντο is the passive of ῥαίνω ‘sprinkle’, and νέρθε is νέρθεν ‘beneath’. τειρόμενον is the participle of τείρω ‘wear down’; βασιλῆα is ‘the king’. φέροντες is plural, though the horses are a pair: the dual of the last unit gives way to the plural. μάχης ἀπάνευθε is ‘apart from the battle’, ἀπάνευθε taking the genitive.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτωρ δ’ ὡς ἐνόησ’ Ἀγαμέμνονα νόσφι κιόντα
Τρωσί τε καὶ Λυκίοισιν ἐκέκλετο μακρὸν ἀΰσας·
sentences.tr:
Hektōr d’ hōs enoēs’ Agamemnona nosphi kionta
Trōsi te kai Lykioisin ekekleto makron aÿsas·
sentences.l:
And Hector, when he noticed Agamemnon going away,
to the Trojans and Lycians called out, shouting loudly:
sentences.i: And when Hector saw Agamemnon going away, he gave orders to the Trojans and Lycians, shouting loudly:
sentences.n: Hector takes his chance and rallies the Trojans and their Lycian allies. ἐνόησ’ is ἐνόησε ‘noticed’, νόσφι is ‘apart, away’, and κιόντα is the participle of κίω ‘go’. ἐκέκλετο is ‘called out to’, from κέλομαι, an old reduplicated aorist, and μακρὸν ἀΰσας is ‘shouting loudly’ (μακρόν is ‘long’ used as an adverb); the line is the same shape as 6.66 and 6.110. The Lycians are allies of Troy from Asia Minor. A speech follows.

sentences.t:
Τρῶες καὶ Λύκιοι καὶ Δάρδανοι ἀγχιμαχηταὶ
ἀνέρες ἔστε φίλοι, μνήσασθε δὲ θούριδος ἀλκῆς.
sentences.tr:
Trōes kai Lykioi kai Dardanoi anchimachētai
aneres este philoi, mnēsasthe de thouridos alkēs.
sentences.l:
“Trojans and Lycians and Dardanians, close-fighters,
men be, friends, and be mindful of impetuous might.
sentences.i: “Trojans and Lycians and Dardanians, fighters at close quarters, be men, friends, and remember impetuous might.
sentences.n: Hector’s speech is a shout to the three peoples of his army and is made of stock phrases; the two lines are word for word the lines of 8.173–174. The Dardanians are a people allied with Troy. ἀγχιμαχηταί is ‘fighters at close quarters’, from ἀγχί ‘near’ and μάχομαι ‘fight’. ἀνέρες ἔστε is ‘be men’ (ἀνέρες is the nominative plural of ἀνήρ, and ἔστε is the imperative of εἰμί): it means ‘be brave’. φίλοι is the vocative ‘friends’. μνήσασθε is the aorist imperative middle of μιμνήσκομαι ‘remember’, with the genitive θούριδος ἀλκῆς ‘impetuous might’. The Greek carries no quotation marks.

sentences.t:
οἴχετ’ ἀνὴρ ὤριστος, ἐμοὶ δὲ μέγ’ εὖχος ἔδωκε
Ζεὺς Κρονίδης·
sentences.tr:
oichet’ anēr ōristos, emoi de meg’ euchos edōke
Zeus Kronidēs·
sentences.l:
He is gone, the man, the best, and to me a great boast has given
Zeus, the son-of-Cronus;
sentences.i: The best man has gone, and Zeus, the son of Cronus, has given me a great triumph;
sentences.n: Hector’s claim: with Agamemnon out of the fight, the Trojans’ best opponent is gone and Zeus has granted a triumph. οἴχετ’ is οἴχεται, ‘is gone’ (οἴχομαι); ὤριστος is ὁ ἄριστος, ‘the best’, with the article and the adjective run together (crasis). εὖχος is ‘boast’ in the word-for-word line, as the thing a man boasts of, and ‘triumph’ in the English. ἔδωκε is the aorist ‘gave’, here ‘has given’, and Ζεὺς Κρονίδης is ‘Zeus, the son of Cronus’. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of line 289.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἰθὺς ἐλαύνετε μώνυχας ἵππους
ἰφθίμων Δαναῶν, ἵν’ ὑπέρτερον εὖχος ἄρησθε.
sentences.tr:
all’ ithys elaunete mōnychas hippous
iphthimōn Danaōn, hin’ hyperteron euchos arēsthe.
sentences.l:
but straight drive the solid-hoofed horses
at the mighty Danaans, that a higher boast you may win.”
sentences.i: but drive your solid-hoofed horses straight at the mighty Danaans, so that you may win a still higher triumph.”
sentences.n: The order that follows from the claim: charge now. ἰθύς is ‘straight’, taking the genitive ἰφθίμων Δαναῶν ‘the mighty Danaans’, and ἐλαύνετε is the imperative ‘drive’. μώνυχας ἵππους is ‘solid-hoofed horses’, μώνυξ meaning with an undivided hoof, and ἰφθίμων ‘mighty’ is the stock epithet. ἵν’ is ‘so that’, and ἄρησθε is the aorist subjunctive middle of ἄρνυμαι ‘win, gain’; ὑπέρτερον is the comparative ‘higher’, ‘a triumph higher than this one’. The speech ends here; the Greek carries no quotation marks.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ὄτρυνε μένος καὶ θυμὸν ἑκάστου.
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn otryne menos kai thymon hekastou.
sentences.l: So having spoken, he urged on the might and the heart of each man.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and urged on the might and the heart of each man.
sentences.n: The speech has ended, and its effect is told at once: each man’s fighting strength is roused. The line is word for word the line of 5.470 and of 6.72. ὣς εἰπών is ‘so having spoken’, ὄτρυνε is the unaugmented aorist of ὀτρύνω ‘urge on’, and μένος καὶ θυμόν ‘might and heart’ is what Hector rouses in ἑκάστου ‘each man’.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε πού τις θηρητὴρ κύνας ἀργιόδοντας
σεύῃ ἐπ’ ἀγροτέρῳ συῒ καπρίῳ ἠὲ λέοντι,
ὣς ἐπ’ Ἀχαιοῖσιν σεῦε Τρῶας μεγαθύμους
Ἕκτωρ Πριαμίδης βροτολοιγῷ ἶσος Ἄρηϊ.
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hote pou tis thērētēr kynas argiodontas
seuēi ep’ agroterōi syï kapriōi ēe leonti,
hōs ep’ Achaioisin seue Trōas megathymous
Hektōr Priamidēs brotoloigōi isos Arēï.
sentences.l:
And as when somewhere a hunter, white-toothed dogs
may set on a wild swine, a boar, or a lion,
so on the Achaeans he set the great-hearted Trojans,
Hector, Priam’s-son, equal to mortal-ruining Ares.
sentences.i: As when a hunter somewhere sets his white-toothed dogs on a wild boar or a lion, so Hector, son of Priam, the equal of Ares, the ruin of mortals, set the great-hearted Trojans on the Achaeans.
sentences.n: A simile for Hector’s attack: the Trojans are the dogs, the Achaeans the quarry, and Hector the hunter. ὡς δ’ ὅτε πού τις … σεύῃ is ‘as when somewhere someone sets on’, with the subjunctive for what happens whenever it happens. ἀργιόδοντας ‘white-toothed’ is said here of dogs. ἀγροτέρῳ is ‘wild’, and συῒ καπρίῳ is ‘swine, boar’; ἠέ is ‘or’. In the second half σεῦε is the imperfect of σεύω ‘set in motion’, with ἐπ’ Ἀχαιοῖσιν ‘against the Achaeans’, and μεγαθύμους ‘great-hearted’ goes with the Trojans. Ἕκτωρ Πριαμίδης ‘Hector, son of Priam’ (Priam’s-son, like Atreus’-son) comes again in the first words of line 300. βροτολοιγῷ ἶσος Ἄρηϊ is ‘equal to Ares, the ruin of mortals’, βροτολοιγός being βροτός ‘mortal’ and λοιγός ‘ruin’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ ἐν πρώτοισι μέγα φρονέων ἐβεβήκει,
ἐν δ’ ἔπεσ’ ὑσμίνῃ ὑπεραέϊ ἶσος ἀέλλῃ,
ἥ τε καθαλλομένη ἰοειδέα πόντον ὀρίνει.
sentences.tr:
autos d’ en prōtoisi mega phroneōn ebebēkei,
en d’ epes’ hysminēi hyperaeï isos aellēi,
hē te kathallomenē ioeidea ponton orinei.
sentences.l:
And he himself among the foremost, greatly thinking, had gone,
and fell upon the battle, equal to a blast blowing from above,
which, leaping down, stirs the violet-dark sea.
sentences.i: He himself went among the foremost, full of proud thoughts, and fell upon the battle like a storm blowing down from above, which leaps down and stirs the violet-dark sea.
sentences.n: Hector goes in with the first rank, and a second simile, the sea under a storm, shows how he strikes. αὐτός ‘he himself’ is set against the men he has just sent forward, and ἐβεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, ‘had gone’, so ‘was in motion’. μέγα φρονέων is ‘greatly thinking’: he is full of proud thoughts. ἐν … ἔπεσ’ is a tmesis (ἐνέπεσε ‘fell upon’), with the dative ὑσμίνῃ ‘battle’. ὑπεραέϊ goes with ἀέλλῃ: it is built from ὑπέρ ‘over’ and the root of ἄημι ‘blow’, and ‘blowing from above’ fits καθαλλομένη ‘leaping down’ in the next line, but the sense of the prefix is not certain. ἄελλα is a storm-blast. ἰοειδέα ‘violet-dark’ is the stock epithet of the sea, and ὀρίνει is ‘stirs up’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα τίνα πρῶτον, τίνα δ’ ὕστατον ἐξενάριξεν
Ἕκτωρ Πριαμίδης, ὅτε οἱ Ζεὺς κῦδος ἔδωκεν;
sentences.tr:
entha tina prōton, tina d’ hystaton exenarixen
Hektōr Priamidēs, hote hoi Zeus kydos edōken;
sentences.l:
Then whom first, and whom last, did he despoil,
Hector, Priam’s-son, when to him Zeus gave glory?
sentences.i: Whom did Hector, son of Priam, first kill and strip of his armour there, and whom last, when Zeus gave him glory?
sentences.n: The poet asks himself a question and then answers it with a list of the dead. ἔνθα is ‘then, there’, and ἐξενάριξεν is ‘killed and stripped’, here as ‘despoiled’. τίνα πρῶτον, τίνα δ’ ὕστατον is ‘whom first, and whom last?’, and ὅτε οἱ Ζεὺς κῦδος ἔδωκεν is ‘when Zeus gave him glory’ (οἱ is ‘to him’). The Greek ends with a Greek question mark, the semicolon.

sentences.t:
Ἀσαῖον μὲν πρῶτα καὶ Αὐτόνοον καὶ Ὀπίτην
καὶ Δόλοπα Κλυτίδην καὶ Ὀφέλτιον ἠδ’ Ἀγέλαον
Αἴσυμνόν τ’ Ὦρόν τε καὶ Ἱππόνοον μενεχάρμην.
sentences.tr:
Asaion men prōta kai Autonoon kai Opitēn
kai Dolopa Klytidēn kai Opheltion ēd’ Agelaon
Aisymnon t’ Ōron te kai Hipponoon menecharmēn.
sentences.l:
Asaeus first, and Autonous, and Opites,
and Dolops, Clytius’-son, and Opheltius and Agelaus,
Aesymnus and Orus and Hipponous, steadfast in the fray.
sentences.i: First Asaeus, and Autonous, and Opites, and Dolops, son of Clytius, and Opheltius and Agelaus, Aesymnus and Orus, and Hipponous, steadfast in the fray.
sentences.n: The answer is a list of nine names, all in the accusative: each is the object of ἐξενάριξεν in line 299, which is not repeated. The next unit says they were leaders of the Danaans. μὲν πρῶτα is ‘first’, Κλυτίδην is the patronymic ‘Clytius’-son’, ἠδ’ is ‘and’, and τε … τε … καί join the last three names. μενεχάρμην ‘steadfast in the fray’ is singular, so it goes with the nearest name, Hipponous; it is built from μένω ‘stand fast’ and χάρμη ‘fight’.

sentences.t:
τοὺς ἄρ’ ὅ γ’ ἡγεμόνας Δαναῶν ἕλεν, αὐτὰρ ἔπειτα
πληθύν, ὡς ὁπότε νέφεα Ζέφυρος στυφελίξῃ
ἀργεστᾶο Νότοιο βαθείῃ λαίλαπι τύπτων·
sentences.tr:
tous ar’ ho g’ hēgemonas Danaōn helen, autar epeita
plēthyn, hōs hopote nephea Zephyros styphelixēi
argestao Notoio batheiēi lailapi typtōn·
sentences.i: These, the leaders of the Danaans, he killed, and after them the mass of the army, as when the West Wind drives before it the clouds of the bright South Wind, striking with a deep squall;
sentences.n: The first two lines finish the list and turn to the common soldiers; the third begins a simile of wind and sea. τοὺς ἄρ’ ὅ γ’ is ‘these, then, he’, and ἡγεμόνας ‘leaders’ stands beside τούς to say what they were. ἕλεν is the aorist of αἱρέω, ‘took’, which in the English becomes ‘killed’. πληθύν is ‘the mass’. In the simile, στυφελίξῃ is the subjunctive of στυφελίζω ‘strike hard, drive’, Ζέφυρος the West Wind, and νέφεα ‘clouds’. ἀργεστᾶο is the epic genitive of an epithet of the South Wind, Νότοιο; its meaning is not known, and ‘bright’ is the usual guess. βαθείῃ λαίλαπι is ‘with a deep squall’, and τύπτων ‘striking’. The unit stops at the raised dot, at the end of line 306.

sentences.t:
πολλὸν δὲ τρόφι κῦμα κυλίνδεται, ὑψόσε δ’ ἄχνη
σκίδναται ἐξ ἀνέμοιο πολυπλάγκτοιο ἰωῆς·
sentences.tr:
pollon de trophi kyma kylindetai, hypsose d’ achnē
skidnatai ex anemoio polyplanktoio iōēs·
sentences.l:
and much, swollen, the wave rolls, and aloft the spray
is scattered by the blast of the much-straying wind;
sentences.i: and the wave rolls on, greatly swollen, and the spray is scattered aloft by the rush of the far-roaming wind;
sentences.n: The simile goes on with the sea driven by the wind: the wave rolls, the spray is thrown into the air. τρόφι is an old word of uncertain sense, taken as ‘swollen, in a mass’, and πολλόν is ‘greatly’. κυλίνδεται is ‘rolls’, and ὑψόσε is ‘upward, aloft’. σκίδναται is ‘is scattered’, ἄχνη is ‘spray’, and ἰωῆς is ‘blast, rush’, here of the wind. πολυπλάγκτοιο is ‘much-straying’ in the word-for-word line, from πλάζω ‘drive astray’, and ‘far-roaming’ in the English. The unit stops at the raised dot, at the end of line 308.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα πυκνὰ καρήαθ’ ὑφ’ Ἕκτορι δάμνατο λαῶν.
sentences.tr: hōs ara pykna karēath’ hyph’ Hektori damnato laōn.
sentences.l: so then thick the heads under Hector were overcome, of the people.
sentences.i: So thickly were the heads of the people overcome beneath Hector.
sentences.n: The simile ends and the comparison is spelled out: the dead fall as thickly as the spray flies. ὣς ἄρα is ‘so then’, πυκνά is ‘thick’ used as an adverb, and καρήαθ’ is καρήατα, the epic plural of κάρη ‘head’, with ‘heads’ standing for the men themselves. δάμνατο is a plural imperfect passive of δάμνημι ‘subdue’ (the epic ending -ατο), and ὑφ’ Ἕκτορι is ‘beneath Hector’, ‘at Hector’s hands’. λαῶν is ‘of the people’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθά κε λοιγὸς ἔην καὶ ἀμήχανα ἔργα γένοντο,
καί νύ κεν ἐν νήεσσι πέσον φεύγοντες Ἀχαιοί,
εἰ μὴ Τυδεΐδῃ Διομήδεϊ κέκλετ’ Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr:
entha ke loigos eēn kai amēchana erga genonto,
kai ny ken en nēessi peson pheugontes Achaioi,
ei mē Tydeïdēi Diomēdeï keklet’ Odysseus·
sentences.i: Then there would have been ruin, and deeds past all remedy would have come to pass, and the Achaeans would have fallen in flight among the ships, if Odysseus had not called on Diomedes, the son of Tydeus:
sentences.n: A turn in the story: the rout would have been complete if one man had not spoken. The first line is word for word 8.130; the second line there is a different one, the Trojans penned in Ilios like lambs. κε with ἔην and γένοντο marks what would have happened and did not; εἰ μή ‘if not’ names what stopped it. ἀμήχανα ἔργα are ‘deeds past help’, and νύ is ‘now, indeed’. πέσον is the aorist of πίπτω ‘fall’, and ἐν νήεσσι πέσον is ‘fall in among the ships’ in headlong flight. κέκλετ’ is κέκλετο, the aorist of κέλομαι ‘call on’, here said of one friend to another, and Τυδεΐδῃ is the patronymic ‘Tydeus’-son’. The unit ends at the raised dot, where the speech begins.

sentences.t: Τυδεΐδη τί παθόντε λελάσμεθα θούριδος ἀλκῆς;
sentences.tr: Tydeïdē ti pathonte lelasmetha thouridos alkēs;
sentences.l: “Tydeus’-son, what having suffered, we two, have we forgotten impetuous might?
sentences.i: “Son of Tydeus, what has come over the two of us, that we have forgotten impetuous might?
sentences.n: Odysseus’ speech begins with a reproach to himself and Diomedes. Τυδεΐδη is the vocative ‘Tydeus’-son’. τί παθόντε is ‘having suffered what?’, the dual participle (‘we two’), and means ‘what has happened to us that…?’. λελάσμεθα is the perfect of λανθάνομαι ‘forget’, which takes the genitive θούριδος ἀλκῆς ‘impetuous might’. The Greek ends with the Greek question mark, the semicolon, and carries no quotation marks.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δεῦρο πέπον, παρ’ ἔμ’ ἵσταο·
sentences.tr: all’ age deuro pepon, par’ em’ histao·
sentences.l: But come, here, good one, beside me stand;
sentences.i: But come here, my good fellow, and stand by me;
sentences.n: The call to stand together. ἀλλ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’, δεῦρο is ‘here’, and πέπον is a friendly form of address whose exact meaning is not known (‘good one’ is the house rendering). παρ’ ἔμ’ is παρὰ ἐμέ ‘beside me’, and ἵσταο is the epic imperative middle of ἵστημι (= Attic ἵστασο), ‘take your stand’. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of line 314.

sentences.t:
δὴ γὰρ ἔλεγχος
ἔσσεται εἴ κεν νῆας ἕλῃ κορυθαίολος Ἕκτωρ.
sentences.tr:
dē gar elenchos
essetai ei ken nēas helēi korythaiolos Hektōr.
sentences.l:
for indeed a disgrace
it will be, if the ships he takes, Hector of the glancing helmet.”
sentences.i: for it will be a disgrace indeed if Hector of the glancing helmet takes the ships.”
sentences.n: The reason to stand: losing the ships would shame them. δὴ γάρ is ‘for indeed’, and ἔλεγχος is ‘disgrace’ (a word for what is said against a man). ἔσσεται is the epic future of εἰμί, ‘will be’, and εἴ κεν … ἕλῃ is ‘if (in case) he takes’, the subjunctive with κεν. κορυθαίολος ‘of the glancing helmet’ is the stock epithet of Hector. The speech ends here; the Greek carries no quotation marks.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη κρατερὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē krateros Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed strong Diomedes:
sentences.i: In answer strong Diomedes said to him:
sentences.n: This is the formula for a reply: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη ‘answering him, he addressed’ with the name of the speaker added at the end. ἀπαμειβόμενος is ‘answering’, the ἀπο- adding ‘in return’; προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘address’. κρατερός ‘strong’ is the stock epithet of Diomedes and is translated every time. A speech follows.

sentences.t: ἤτοι ἐγὼ μενέω καὶ τλήσομαι·
sentences.tr: ētoi egō meneō kai tlēsomai·
sentences.l: “Indeed I shall stay and endure;
sentences.i: “I will stay, indeed, and endure;
sentences.n: Diomedes agrees, but he grants only half: the next words say that it will not help for long. ἤτοι is printed as one word, ‘indeed, it is true that’, and it is answered by the ἀλλά that begins the next unit. μενέω is the epic future of μένω ‘stay, hold firm’ and τλήσομαι the future of τλῆναι ‘endure’. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of line 317.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ μίνυνθα
ἡμέων ἔσσεται ἦδος, ἐπεὶ νεφεληγερέτα Ζεὺς
Τρωσὶν δὴ βόλεται δοῦναι κράτος ἠέ περ ἡμῖν.
sentences.tr:
alla minyntha
hēmeōn essetai ēdos, epei nephelēgereta Zeus
Trōsin dē boletai dounai kratos ēe per hēmin.
sentences.l:
but for a short time
of us there will be enjoyment, since cloud-gatherer Zeus
to the Trojans indeed wishes to give strength rather than to us.”
sentences.i: but the pleasure of having us will be short, since Zeus who gathers the clouds wishes to give the Trojans the strength, rather than us.”
sentences.n: The reason it will not help for long: Zeus is for the Trojans. μίνυνθα is ‘for a short time’, and ἡμέων is the epic genitive of ἡμεῖς ‘us’. ἦδος is ‘pleasure, satisfaction’ and with the genitive means the pleasure to be had of us; the thought is that their standing firm will bring the Achaeans little, but how exactly it is meant is not certain. ἐπεὶ … νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς is ‘since cloud-gatherer Zeus’, the stock epithet translated every time. βόλεται is the epic form of βούλεται ‘wishes’, and δοῦναι κράτος is ‘to give strength’, κράτος including the upper hand; ἠέ περ ἡμῖν is ‘rather than to us’. The speech ends here; the Greek carries no quotation marks.

sentences.t:
ἦ καὶ Θυμβραῖον μὲν ἀφ’ ἵππων ὦσε χαμᾶζε
δουρὶ βαλὼν κατὰ μαζὸν ἀριστερόν·
sentences.tr:
ē kai Thymbraion men aph’ hippōn ōse chamaze
douri balōn kata mazon aristeron·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and Thymbraeus from the horses thrust to the ground,
with spear having struck him on the left breast;
sentences.i: So he said, and struck Thymbraeus with his spear on the left breast, and thrust him from his chariot to the ground;
sentences.n: Diomedes acts at once. ἦ καί is ‘he spoke, and’, ἦ being ‘he said’, and the pair means that the deed follows the word. Θυμβραῖον is the accusative of Θυμβραῖος, Thymbraeus, a man named only here in this part. ἀφ’ ἵππων is ‘from the horses’, that is from his chariot. ὦσε is the aorist of ὠθέω ‘push’, and χαμᾶζε is ‘to the ground’. δουρὶ βαλών is ‘having struck with a spear’, and κατὰ μαζὸν ἀριστερόν is ‘at the left breast’. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of line 321.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἀντίθεον θεράποντα Μολίονα τοῖο ἄνακτος.
sentences.tr:
autar Odysseus
antitheon theraponta Moliona toio anaktos.
sentences.l:
but Odysseus
the godlike attendant Molion, of that lord.
sentences.i: while Odysseus struck down Molion, the godlike attendant of that lord.
sentences.n: Odysseus does the same to the attendant. The verb is not repeated: Μολίονα is the object of a verb understood from line 320, and the English supplies ‘struck down’. αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεύς ‘but Odysseus’ answers the μέν of 320, ‘on the one hand…’. ἀντίθεον is ‘godlike’ and θεράποντα is ‘attendant’, and τοῖο ἄνακτος ‘of that lord’ is the epic genitive of the pronoun with ἄναξ: the attendant of Thymbraeus.

sentences.t: τοὺς μὲν ἔπειτ’ εἴασαν, ἐπεὶ πολέμου ἀπέπαυσαν·
sentences.tr: tous men epeit’ eiasan, epei polemou apepausan·
sentences.l: These then they left, since from war they had made them cease;
sentences.i: Those two they then left, now that they had put an end to their fighting;
sentences.n: To ‘make someone cease from war’ is a plain way of saying they killed them. τοὺς μὲν is ‘these’, the two just struck down, and εἴασαν is the aorist of ἐάω, which with a plain object means ‘left’. ἐπεὶ … ἀπέπαυσαν is ‘since they had made them stop’, from ἀποπαύω with the genitive πολέμου ‘from war’.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἀν’ ὅμιλον ἰόντε κυδοίμεον, ὡς ὅτε κάπρω
ἐν κυσὶ θηρευτῇσι μέγα φρονέοντε πέσητον·
sentences.tr:
tō d’ an’ homilon ionte kydoimeon, hōs hote kaprō
en kysi thēreutēisi mega phroneonte pesēton·
sentences.l:
and the two, through the throng going, were making uproar, as when two boars
among hunting dogs, greatly thinking, fall;
sentences.i: and the two of them went through the throng making an uproar of battle, like two boars, full of proud thoughts, that fall in among hunting dogs;
sentences.n: Odysseus and Diomedes are now compared to two boars that fall in among hunting dogs. The words for the two men and the two boars are in the dual: τὼ ‘the two’, ἰόντε ‘going’, κάπρω ‘two boars’, φρονέοντε ‘thinking’, πέσητον ‘fall’; κυδοίμεον is plural, a plural verb for the pair. κυδοίμεον is the imperfect of κυδοιμέω ‘make an uproar, throw into confusion’, from κυδοιμός ‘the din of battle’, and ἀν’ ὅμιλον is ‘through the throng’. ὡς ὅτε … πέσητον is ‘as when … fall’, with the subjunctive for what happens whenever it happens. θηρευτῇσι is ‘hunting’, said of the dogs, and μέγα φρονέοντε is ‘greatly thinking’, here again proud and confident.

sentences.t: ὣς ὄλεκον Τρῶας πάλιν ὀρμένω·
sentences.tr: hōs olekon Trōas palin ormenō·
sentences.l: So they were destroying the Trojans, rushing back;
sentences.i: So the two of them, rushing back into the fray, destroyed the Trojans;
sentences.n: The comparison is spelled out and the action goes on. ὄλεκον is the imperfect of ὀλέκω ‘destroy’, a plural verb for the pair, and πάλιν ὀρμένω is ‘rushing back’, with the dual participle of ὄρνυμι in the middle voice. The unit stops at the raised dot, in the middle of line 326.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὶ
ἀσπασίως φεύγοντες ἀνέπνεον Ἕκτορα δῖον.
sentences.tr:
autar Achaioi
aspasiōs pheugontes anepneon Hektora dion.
sentences.l:
but the Achaeans,
gladly fleeing, breathed again from heavenly Hector.
sentences.i: while the Achaeans, fleeing from heavenly Hector, drew breath again with joy.
sentences.n: The part closes on the relief of the fleeing Achaeans. ἀσπασίως is ‘gladly’, and φεύγοντες Ἕκτορα δῖον is ‘fleeing from heavenly Hector’: φεύγω takes the accusative of the one fled from, though the word order also lets Ἕκτορα be read with ἀνέπνεον. ἀνέπνεον is the imperfect of ἀναπνέω ‘draw breath again, recover’. δῖος ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet.
